transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendoza (CTO - Atlas), Elena Park (Eng Manager), Mark Rivera (SRE), Nina Cho (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, might be incomplete):
- Walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, request logs, and error analysis flows.
- Discussed how to correlate traces to request logs, SLO monitoring, and debugging flow for token-level errors and model fallbacks.
- Customer interested in private deployment and audit requirements; asked about KMS, SSO and data retention.
- Agreed next steps: security docs, sample logs/traces, bench run of request profile.

Topics: tracing, request logs export, error analysis, KV cache/latency, private/VPC considerations, SOC2/KMS, rollout/fallbacks

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan with Redwood, AE for the account. Today Priya and I will walk through the Console tracing and error analysis flows, and show how request logs tie into traces. Quick intro, Priya?
[00:10] Priya: Hi all, Priya Kapoor, I'm a solutions engineer. I'll show the tracing UI and a few examples—latency hotspots, error grouping, and request-log joins.
[00:18] Carlos: Great. We're mostly interested in how we debug production LLM errors, and how to triage cost vs latency. We've seen noisy failures in inference pipelines.
[00:26] Jordan: Perfect. Quick agenda: open the Console, demo a live trace, show request logs, then show error analysis and an example of a canary fallback. We'll leave time for questions.
[00:35] Elena: Sounds good. One ask up front — any notes on data residency and KMS? Nina will have a few compliance Qs.
[00:41] Nina: Yes, we need to know where logs live, retention, and whether keys are customer-managed.
[00:47] Jordan: We'll cover that at the end; we also will attach the SOC2 packet after.

[01:05] Priya: Ok, switching screens now. (screen share) This is the Redwood Console main page — route overview, model health. I'm going to the traces tab. Note: UI is slightly different depending on dedicated vs hosted but flow is same.
[01:20] Priya: Here you can see a list of recent traces, they're auto-sampled and also can be pulled from request logs. I'll filter to errors and timeout spikes. You can see percentiles and a small flamegraph for a single request.
[01:34] Mark: Is that sample rate configurable? We have pretty spiky traffic; we don't want to miss rare timeouts.
[01:40] Priya: Yes — sampling is configurable per-route. For Dedicated we can keep higher sample rates; for hosted we recommend adaptive sampling to keep storage costs down. There's also smart prefix sampling for warm KV cache hits.
[01:54] Carlos: You mentioned KV cache — can we see cache hit/miss in the trace?
[01:58] Priya: Yep, trace spans include cache hits/misses as span attributes. Sometimes transcriber shows K V cache as separate words — but it's the same. You can group by attribute 'kv_hit' to isolate cold starts.

[02:20] Priya: I'll open a trace that shows a tail-latency event. (opens trace) Top shows the timeline with model inference spans and network spans. Here we have a long span in the backend model call — if you expand you can see token-level timing and the exact request id.
[02:40] Priya: Now the important bit: join this to request logs. Click 'join logs' and select timeframe. The Console will fetch request-log entries for the request id; you can see prompt, token usage, model variant, route config, and any retry attempts.
[02:56] Elena: How much of the prompt is stored? We have PII concerns.
[03:00] Priya: By default, we store metadata and anonymized prompts for debugging; full prompts are optional and can be disabled — in Private mode you can choose to never persist prompts. We'll share the retention/KMS docs.

[03:20] Jordan: Quick pause — customer question about encryption?
[03:23] Nina: Do you support customer-managed KMS and HSM? Also SAML SSO for Console access?
[03:29] Jordan: Yes on both. For Private we integrate with customer KMS, and Console access can be SAML SSO with RBAC. We'll send the integration docs.

[03:48] Priya: Back to the trace. So here's an error: you see 'token generation error' and a 500 from the runtime. We group similar errors and assign an error fingerprint so you see frequency. The error view surfaces the stack, the route config, and any recent model rollouts that coincide with the spike.
[04:06] Mark: Can you correlate errors with model variant or quantization changes? We did a quantize patch last week.
[04:11] Priya: Yes, the trace shows the model artifact id and quantization profile. You can filter errors by model version and by serving node.

[04:28] Priya: Another useful flow is the request-log replay. For any request id you can replay against a different model variant in a sandbox. This helps validate rollouts without impacting prod.
[04:40] Carlos: That replay — does it use real tokens and count against billing?
[04:44] Priya: Replays are sandboxed and you can choose whether to bill. For privacy we recommend replays on sanitized prompts or in Private mode. We'll show a quick replay demo.

[04:58] Priya: Starting replay... here's the comparison view: original latency, new latency, and token differences. If you see a regression, Console can automatically flag the rollout and rollback if configured.
[05:12] Jordan: On the topic of rollouts — you can set canary rules by percent, and tie thresholds to error rate or token-cost increases. If threshold hit, we can auto-fallback to a cheaper variant.
[05:24] Elena: Do you expose token-level costs in the trace? We want per-request cost breakdown.
[05:29] Priya: Yes, the request-log includes a token_count and estimated cost breakdown. Console shows cost delta when comparing variants.

[05:42] Priya: Now I'll show error grouping. This groups by fingerprint and shows first-seen vs last-seen and a sample trace. Common causes are model timeouts, malformed prompts, or KV cache misses that cause cold starts.
[05:58] Mark: How does Redwood detect malformed prompts? Sometimes downstream clients send JSON-with-newline and it breaks the model parse.
[06:05] Priya: We don't parse semantics but we surface input anomalies — tokenization anomalies and unexpected control tokens are flagged. You can create rules to bubble critical anomalies to your SRE channel.

[06:20] Jordan: Quick interjection — pricing question?
[06:23] Carlos: Yes, curious how request-log retention affects cost.
[06:26] Jordan: We price request-log storage separately; Dedicated customers can opt for longer retention at negotiated rates. Optimize also gives recommendations for sampling rates and batching to lower unit costs.

[06:45] Priya: Now request log export. You can export logs as newline-delimited JSON; we also have direct S3 delivery for Dedicated/Private. Here I'm exporting a 2-day sample. (exports)
[06:57] Priya: Exports include request_id, route, model_version, token counts, error codes, and anonymized prompt unless full text is enabled.
[07:08] Nina: Is there a way to redaction on export? We need to remove email addresses and PII automatically.
[07:12] Priya: Yes, we have configurable redaction rules. For Private you can inject a custom redaction lambda before export.

[07:26] Elena: About tracing overhead — do traces add latency? We worry about payer impact.
[07:32] Priya: Tracing is asynchronous — span collection is buffered and shipped; it adds minimal tail latency. Heavy sampling or token-level tracing can increase overhead, so we recommend sampled token-level only for canaries.

[07:50] Priya: I'll open the 'errors timeline' dashboard. This aggregates error rate by route and model. You can pin an alert to Slack, PagerDuty.
[08:02] Carlos: Can the alert include contextual links to the trace and the request-log export?
[08:06] Priya: Absolutely — alerts include deep links to a representative trace and the request-log query.

[08:18] Priya: One more feature: interactive debugging flow. You can jump from the error group to a suggested runbook. Runbooks are editable and can contain steps and a checklist for oncall. You can attach a runbook to an automated remediation.
[08:34] Mark: Nice. Would that integrate with our incident response runbooks in Opsgenie?
[08:38] Jordan: We have webhook integrations and can push incidents into Opsgenie/PagerDuty.

[08:50] Elena: For the private deployment questions — can we host the tracing collector inside our VPC and never send spans to Redwood?
[08:58] Priya: Yes — in Private mode the control plane can run in your VPC and logs/traces can be kept on-prem. There's an on-prem collector that writes to your S3 or internal object store.

[09:12] Carlos: About audit logs and access controls — we need detailed who-did-what. Does Console store admin actions?
[09:18] Jordan: Yes, audit logs capture Console actions, API keys, who toggled a rollout, etc. They're exportable and integrate with SIEM.

[09:36] Priya: Quick demo of a real incident: here's a trace where the runtime returned a 'model OOM' on a large prompt. The error is grouped; the suggestion was to reduce max tokens or increase batch-size or switch to a model variant with higher memory.
[09:52] Carlos: If we hit OOMs, can Redwood auto-fallback to a lower-memory variant?
[09:57] Priya: Yes, fallback rules can be configured by error fingerprint and have a staged rollout. We also surface a suggested quantization profile.

[10:12] Jordan: Any other questions on tracing before we move to request-log debugging?
[10:16] Elena: When you export logs, can we map the request_id to our internal customer user ids? We have privacy needs but also need correlation.
[10:24] Priya: You can pass in custom metadata fields (an external_id) on each request; those are stored in request logs if you enable them. For PII you can store hashed identifiers.

[10:40] Priya: Now I'll show a quick debug flow: step 1, find error group; step 2, pick representative trace; step 3, join request logs; step 4, run a replay; step 5, open runbook and either remediate or schedule rollback.
[10:58] Priya: I'll demonstrate with a malformed JSON example — you can see tokenization error flagged, and the sample prompt shows the offending payload.
[11:12] Mark: Could we automate patch to server-side preprocessor to sanitize inputs?
[11:15] Priya: Sure — we have a webhook that can call a sanitizer or trigger a lambda. This is often used in Dedicated/Private setups.

[11:30] Carlos: For the performance benchmarks, would you run our traffic profile? We want to see latency/cost on our typical requests.
[11:36] Jordan: Yes, that's part of the pilot — Priya will run a bench with your sample traces and return a report with recommendations on batching, quantization, and prefix caching.

[11:50] Priya: I'll note some immediate recommendations based on today's view: increase prefix KV caching, enable adaptive batching for short prompts, and set token limits & fallback for large prompts. We'll include config snippets.

[12:05] Nina: Last compliance question — retention windows for request logs for hosted customers?
[12:10] Jordan: Hosted defaults to 30 days for request logs, 90 days for traces metadata; Dedicated can be negotiated and Private you control it.

[12:25] Elena: Ok, anything else on automation or observability?
[12:28] Priya: We also have Optimize suggestions — it will analyze your traffic and propose batching and model profiles to hit cost/latency targets. That integrates into Console as a recommendations panel.

[12:40] Carlos: About support SLAs for Dedicated — response times and incident bridges?
[12:44] Jordan: We have SLA tiers; enterprise paid tier includes 1-hour incident response and named support. We'll add that to the follow-up email.

[12:58] Priya: Wrapping up demo — recap of next steps: we'll share SOC2, KMS integration docs, runbench with sample traces, and send recording.
[13:10] Jordan: Great. Any final Qs?
[13:15] Nina: No more from compliance, thanks.
[13:18] Carlos: Thanks — this was helpful. We'll share the logs.
[13:22] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and the action items.

End of transcript.
